userPrompt: Can a company in the EU refuse to give an employee their statutory annual leave?
responseText:
**No, a company in the EU cannot lawfully refuse an employee their statutory annual leave.**

### Key rules under the EU Working Time Directive (2003/88/EC)
- Every worker is entitled to **at least 4 weeks (20 working days)** of paid annual leave per year.
- This right is mandatory and cannot be waived by contract, collective agreement, or employer decision.
- The employer **must** allow the employee to take the leave.

### What the employer can and cannot do
| Action | Lawful? | Notes |
|--------|---------|-------|
| Refuse to grant the statutory minimum leave | No | Strictly prohibited |
| Unilaterally decide when leave is taken | Yes | With due regard to business needs and employee interests |
| Require the employee to take leave during a specific period (e.g. factory shutdown) | Usually yes | Common practice if reasonable notice is given |
| Pay out unused leave instead of granting it (except on termination) | Generally no | Leave must be taken; cash in lieu is only allowed when employment ends |
| Carry over unused leave to the next year | Only in limited cases | Usually only if the employee was unable to take it for reasons beyond their control (e.g. long-term sickness). Many Member States allow carry-over by agreement. |

### Practical consequences if an employer refuses
- The employee can enforce the right through national labour courts or authorities.
- Refusal can lead to financial penalties for the company and compensation for the employee (including payment for untaken leave plus damages).
- In most EU countries the right is also protected by national constitutions or human-rights provisions.

**Bottom line:** An EU employer may schedule or postpone statutory leave within legal limits, but it cannot simply refuse to grant the minimum 4 weeks of paid annual leave. If this is happening, the employee should document the refusal and seek advice from the national labour inspectorate, works council, or a lawyer.
